newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia, US see progress on arms, differ on Baltics.
newsitem.headline: Russia, US see progress on arms, differ on Baltics.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright left Russia on Sunday saying she had "wonderful" talks with Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov but the two remain far apart on some issues despite progress on others.

The two diplomats, who have built up a considerable rapport despite months of fierce duelling over NATO expansion, agreed to extend talks on revising a European arms control pact but clashed over issues in Bosnia and the Baltic states.

"There were not entirely coinciding points of view," the unflappable Primakov told Russian news agencies, referring to Albright's rejection of Moscow's opposition to the three small former Soviet states on the Baltic joining NATO.

"We are against the entry of the Baltic states into the North Atlantic alliance," Primakov said as he left St Petersburg. Albright and he held several hours of talks in the Russian Baltic port on Saturday evening and Sunday morning.

Albright had earlier told Russian television: "We have said all along that NATO is open to all democratic market systems in Europe...It doesn't matter where a country is on the map, they are eligible for membership in NATO."

After meeting Primakov, she headed for the Lithuanian capital Vilnius, where she was due to meet ministers from the Baltic states -- Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia. She is expected to reassure them they will not be excluded from NATO.

Primakov, who led vociferous Russian resistance to last week's NATO decision to extend membership invitations to three former Soviet allies -- Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic -- said Moscow was prepared to guarantee the security of the Baltic states, which Stalin seized during World War Two.
Russia has said it may tear up a recently signed charter of cooperation with its former Cold War adversary if any former Soviet republic is admitted to the alliance.

Saying he believed Washington understood Russia's position, Primakov advocated a system of Russian or multilateral guarantees to ensure the Baltic countries' independence and was not against their membership of other European bodies.
On Saturday over dinner in the old tsarist capital, Albright and Primakov crossed swords over Bosnia. Russia denounced NATO's swoop on suspected war criminals last week a "cowboy raid".
Albright pointedly asked if Primakov had any better idea how to bring war criminals to justice, U.S. officials said.
More constructively, Primakov said the two agreed to extend the end of the latest round of European arms control talks in Vienna from July 17 to the end of the month.
"I think we will be able to get some intermediate document which will set down the agreements already reached but at the same time mark the problems," Primakov said on Sunday.

He noted Washington and Moscow alone could not settle the 30-nation talks, aimed at revising the 1990 Conventional Forces in Europe (CFE) treaty after the collapse of the Soviet Union: "But...they might give a boost to speed up the process."
Despite their various differences, both sides stressed cooperation not confrontation was the order of the day.
"We have taken some not unimportant steps towards settling international problems," Primakov said. "Today it's very important to make sure those efforts don't go to waste."

Albright said relations with Russia were "on a very strong basis". Presidents Bill Clinton and Boris Yeltsin were "working very hard to show that there is a new Russia that works with the United States together for peace and security", she said.
